611.quote_or_event: “One cannot quickly arrive at discernment; therefore one should exert one's self, abstain from pleasures, understand the world, be impartial like a sage, and guard one's self: (thus) never be careless.”
611.explanation: The sutra admits the goal is hard and slow to reach, but takes that as a reason to exert oneself, not to give up.
611.tie_back: As the Kural says never to lose heart by calling a task too hard, because effort brings the strength to finish it, the Jain text answers difficulty with steady self-exertion.
611._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Close in spirit (difficulty calls for exertion); the Jain aim is spiritual discernment rather than worldly success.

612.quote_or_event: “You have crossed the great ocean; why do you halt so near the shore? make haste to get on the other side; Gautama, &c.”
612.explanation: Mahavira tells Gautama not to slacken when the goal is nearly won: stopping near the shore wastes the whole crossing.
612.tie_back: The Kural's warning not to let effort slacken halfway, since the world abandons those who leave work unfinished, is matched by Mahavira's rebuke for halting near the shore.
612._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. A strong parallel on not slackening before the task is done; the Kural's point about losing the world's regard is absent.

613.quote_or_event: “doing service consists in giving one's assistance as well as one is able.”
613.explanation: Vaiyāvṛttya, active service to teachers, the sick, the aged and the community, is one of the internal austerities in Jainism; benefiting others is defined as giving one's own exertion.
613.tie_back: The Kural roots the ability to help others in hard work; Jain vaiyāvṛttya likewise defines service as giving active effort as far as one is able.
613._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Only a next-best match: it ties service to personal effort but does not say, as the Kural does, that diligence is the foundation of generosity.

614.quote_or_event: “A man believes himself a hero as long as he does not behold the foe … So a novice, who as yet has not suffered pains and is not yet used to a mendicant's life, believes himself a hero till he practises austerities.”
614.explanation: The Sutrakritanga mocks those who think themselves heroes until real hardship comes; the weak then 'become disheartened like cowards in the battle' (I.3.1.7).
614.tie_back: Valluvar's would-be benefactor who will not work is like a coward holding a sword; the Jain novice who boasts until real effort is needed is the same empty heroism.
614.source: Sutrakritanga I.3.1.1 and I.3.1.3; cf. I.3.1.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
614._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (ellipsis drops the Śiśupāla comparison). The battlefield-coward image matches closely; the link to generosity in particular is missing.

615.quote_or_event: “During his reign he taught, for the benefit of the people, the seventy-two sciences, of which writing is the first, arithmetic the most important, and the knowledge of omens the last, the sixty-four accomplishments of women, the hundred arts, and the three occupations of men.”
615.explanation: Jain tradition honours Rishabha, the first Tirthankara and first king, for teaching people the crafts and occupations that let them make a living, before he renounced the world.
615.tie_back: The Kural's worker who wants work over pleasure and becomes a pillar holding up his kin is mirrored, on a civilisational scale, by Rishabha's labours that held up his people.
615.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha §211 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
615._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. A reasonable but partial match: Rishabha is a model of work that sustains others, but the Kural's contrast between personal pleasure and toil is not explicit.

616.quote_or_event: “Saddalaputta, is your ware made by dint of exertion and manly strength, or on the other hand, is it made without exertion and manly strength?”
616.explanation: Mahavira asks the Ajivika potter Saddalaputta this question to refute Gosala's fatalism (niyati), which denied any role to exertion. The potter's own reactions show that he really does believe effort and conduct make things happen, and he becomes a Jain lay follower.
616.tie_back: The Kural says effort creates prosperity; Mahavira makes the same point by showing that even the potter's prosperous trade depends on 'exertion and manly strength'.
616.source: Uvasagadasao (Upāsakadaśāḥ), ch. 7, Saddalaputta (tr. A.F.R. Hoernle), as quoted in the jainworld.com chapter 'Rival Sects'
616._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the jainworld.com page, which quotes Hoernle's translation; I did not check it against Hoernle's 1888 edition itself. This is a canonical Jain argument for effort against fatalism, very close to the Kural.

617.quote_or_event: Jain tradition knows the goddess Śrī (Lakṣmī) seated on a lotus: she is the fourth of the fourteen auspicious dreams Queen Triśalā saw before Mahavira's birth. But Jain doctrine credits fortune and misfortune to a person's own karma and conduct, not to goddesses of luck.
617.explanation: Jainism keeps Śrī as an auspicious symbol, but in its non-theistic karma theory prosperity and adversity follow one's own deeds, a view close to Valluvar's actual point about effort and sloth.
617.tie_back: The Kural's image of the lotus goddess living in effort and Misfortune living in sloth fits Jainism only as metaphor: in Jain teaching one's own conduct, not a deity, brings fortune.
617.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §36 (the dream of the goddess Śrī) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
617._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from general knowledge of the Kalpa Sutra's dream list; I did not recheck the section number this session. A weak, next-best match: the Kural's two folk goddesses have no real doctrinal counterpart in Jainism.

618.quote_or_event: “Acknowledging the truth about bondage and liberation, but talking only, not acting (in accordance with these tenets), they seek comfort for themselves in mighty words. Clever talking will not work salvation…”
618.explanation: Mahavira condemns those who know the truth but do not act on it; knowledge without exertion saves no one.
618.tie_back: The Kural's real disgrace, knowing what should be done and not making the effort, is exactly the 'false ascetic' of Uttaradhyayana 6, who knows but does not act.
618._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. A close match on knowing but not acting; the Kural's other half, that ill luck is no disgrace, is not covered.

619.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra teaches that austerity (tapas) brings about both the stopping of new karma (saṃvara) and the shedding of karma already bound (nirjarā). For Jains, effort always bears fruit at the level of karma, even when an outward aim fails because of past karma that is ripening.
619.explanation: In Jain doctrine 'fate' is the ripening of one's own past karma; it may block a present goal, but sincere exertion is never wasted, because it wears away karma.
619.tie_back: As the Kural says effort pays the wages of the body's toil even when fate denies the goal, Jainism holds that exertion always earns its return in shed karma.
619.source: Tattvartha Sutra 9.3 (tapasā nirjarā ca); see Nathmal Tatia, That Which Is (1994)
619._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sutra; I did not open Tatia's wording this session. A reasonable doctrinal parallel, though Jain 'fate' is self-made karma, not Parimelazhagar's ūḻ.

620.quote_or_event: “As a large tank, when its supply of water has been stopped, gradually dries up by the consumption of the water and by evaporation, so the Karman of a monk, which he acquired in millions of births, is annihilated by austerities, if there is no influx of bad Karman.”
620.explanation: Jainism teaches that persistent, untiring austerity can wear away even karma built up over countless lives, so no 'destiny' is beyond the reach of effort.
620.tie_back: The Kural's tireless strivers who see fate turn its back match the Jain teaching that unflagging exertion drains away the accumulated karma that makes up one's fate.
620._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (footnote marker removed). A strong doctrinal parallel on effort overcoming accumulated destiny; the image is a drying tank, not a retreating enemy, and the effort is spiritual austerity.
